q-37314.name: Question 1
q-37314.problem:
Find a $2\times 2$ matrix $F$ that has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=4$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ and corresponding eigenvectors

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}5 \\ -4\end{aligned}]
$$
q-37314.worked_solution:
Since $B=\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2}\}$ is a basis of ${R}^{2}$ consisting of the eigenvectors of $F,$ then $F$ must be diagonalizable.

So, we can write $F=PD{P}^{-1},$ where $P$ is a matrix whose columns are the eigenvectors of $F,$ and $D$ is a diagonal matrix whose entries are the eigenvalues in the corresponding order:

$$
F={{[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {v}_{1} & {v}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1} & 0 \\ 0 & {\lambda }_{2}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{{[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {v}_{1} & {v}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

Let $P=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 5 \\ 1 & -4\end{aligned}].$ Then, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}-1 & 5 \\ 1 & -4\end{aligned}]}^{-1}=\frac{1}{-1}[\begin{aligned}-4 & -5 \\ -1 & -1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}4 & 5 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, carrying out the necessary matrix multiplication, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}F & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 5 \\ 1 & -4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & 5 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-4 & -10 \\ 4 & 8\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & 5 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-26 & -30 \\ 24 & 28\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

q-37601.worked_solution:
We have been given the following diagonalization of $M.$

$$
M={{[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}\sqrt[8]{2} & 0 \\ 0 & \sqrt[4]{2}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{{[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

So, since $M=PD{P}^{-1}$, we can compute ${M}^{k}$ by using the formula 

$$
{M}^{k}=P{D}^{k}{P}^{-1}.
$$

First, we find the inverse of the matrix $P.$ We get

$$
{[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]}^{-1}=\frac{1}{1}[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Carrying out the necessary multiplication, we obtain the following:

 

$$
\begin{aligned}{M}^{16} & =P{D}^{16}{P}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}\sqrt[8]{2} & 0 \\ 0 & \sqrt[4]{2}\end{aligned}]}^{16}[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}(\sqrt[8]{2})^{16} & 0 \\ 0 & (\sqrt[4]{2})^{16}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{2}^{2} & 0 \\ 0 & {2}^{4}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 1 & 2\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 16\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}8 & 48 \\ 4 & 32\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-32 & 72 \\ -24 & 52\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

q-37623.problem:
Find a $2\times 2$ matrix $G$ that has eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=6$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=8,$ and corresponding eigenvectors

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3\end{aligned}],\,{v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 5\end{aligned}].
$$
q-37623.worked_solution:
Since $B=\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2}\}$ is a basis of ${R}^{2}$ consisting of the eigenvectors of $G,$ then $G$ must be diagonalizable.

So, we can write $G=PD{P}^{-1},$ where $P$ is a matrix whose columns are the eigenvectors of $G,$ and $D$ is a diagonal matrix whose entries are the eigenvalues in the corresponding order:

$$
G={{[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {v}_{1} & {v}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1} & 0 \\ 0 & {\lambda }_{2}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{{[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {v}_{1} & {v}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

Let $P=[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 3 & 5\end{aligned}].$ Then, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 3 & 5\end{aligned}]}^{-1}=\frac{1}{1}[\begin{aligned}5 & -3 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}5 & -3 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, carrying out the necessary matrix multiplication, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}G & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 \\ 3 & 5\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}6 & 0 \\ 0 & 8\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}5 & -3 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}12 & 24 \\ 18 & 40\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}5 & -3 \\ -3 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-12 & 12 \\ -30 & 26\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

v1=[23],v2=[35].

EXPLANATION

Since B={v1,v2} is a basis of R2 consisting of the eigenvectors of G, then G must be diagonalizable.

So, we can write G=PDP−1, where P is a matrix whose columns are the eigenvectors of G, and D is a diagonal matrix whose entries are the eigenvalues in the corresponding order:

G=[||v1v2||]⏟P[λ100λ2]⏟D[||v1v2||]−1⏟P−1

Let P=[2335]. Then,

P−1=[2335]−1=11[5−3−32]=[5−3−32].

Therefore, carrying out the necessary matrix multiplication, we obtain

G=[2335][6008][5−3−32]=[12241840][5−3−32]=[−1212−3026].

We have been given the following diagonalization of $A.$

$$
A={{[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 0 & -6\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{{[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 0 & -6\end{aligned}]}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

So, since $A=PD{P}^{-1}$, we can compute ${A}^{k}$ by using the formula 

$$
{A}^{k}=P{D}^{k}{P}^{-1}.
$$

First, we find the inverse of the matrix $P.$ We get

$$
{[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 0 & -6\end{aligned}]}^{-1}=\frac{1}{12}[\begin{aligned}-6 & -2 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}].
$$

Carrying out the necessary multiplication, we obtain the following:

 

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{69} & =P{D}^{69}{P}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 0 & -6\end{aligned}]{[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]}^{69}{[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 0 & -6\end{aligned}]}^{-1} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 0 & -6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{1}^{69} & 0 \\ 0 & (-1)^{69}\end{aligned}](\frac{1}{12}[\begin{aligned}-6 & -2 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]) \\  & =\frac{1}{12}[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 0 & -6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-6 & -2 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{12}[\begin{aligned}-2 & -2 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}-6 & -2 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & \frac{2}{3} \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Since $B=\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2}\}$ is a basis of ${R}^{2}$ consisting of the eigenvectors of $S,$ then $S$ must be diagonalizable.

So, we can write $S=PD{P}^{-1},$ where $P$ is a matrix whose columns are the eigenvectors of $S,$ and $D$ is a diagonal matrix whose entries are the eigenvalues in the corresponding order:

$$
S={{[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {v}_{1} & {v}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{P}{{[\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1} & 0 \\ 0 & {\lambda }_{2}\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{D}{{{[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {v}_{1} & {v}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]}^{-1}}_{⏟}}_{{P}^{-1}}
$$

Let $P=[\begin{aligned}6 & 1 \\ 5 & 1\end{aligned}].$ Then, 

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}^{-1} & ={[\begin{aligned}6 & 1 \\ 5 & 1\end{aligned}]}^{-1}=\frac{1}{1}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -5 & 6\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -5 & 6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

 

Therefore, carrying out the necessary matrix multiplication, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =[\begin{aligned}6 & 1 \\ 5 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -5 & 6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}18 & 1 \\ 15 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -5 & 6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}13 & -12 \\ 10 & -9\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$
